text:
Niagara Falls

title: What a chart can tell me
text:
One choice that matters
In a comparison of income and life expectancy, a logarithmic income axis changes the spacing of the values. That can help reveal patterns that are difficult to see when a few large values stretch the scale.

title: What a chart can tell me
section: What I still need to ask
text:
What I still need to ask
A visible association does not explain why the pattern exists. Before moving from description to explanation, I need to think about the research question, the data, and possible alternative explanations.
My next step is to describe the plot in one careful sentence, then write down a question it cannot answer.

A project I’m developing

Comparing life expectancy across countries
COURSE PROJECT · IN PROGRESS
Question. How does life expectancy vary with income across countries in a given year?
Approach. Use R to explore the historical Gapminder data and make a clearly labeled visualization.
What I’m learning. Choosing the year, scale, and unit of analysis changes what readers can see. An association in a plot is a starting point for questions, not evidence of a causal effect.

title: Art Gallery
text:
Good Parenting
Oil on Canvas, 2024
I made this piece to express my gratitude for my dad. My dad has supported me in all my pursuits even when I have stumbled or changed direction. Despite living in a different state than me for most of my life, he has always made every effort to be there for me. He moved in the first place to take a higher paying job and secure a good education for my brother and I. While applying to colleges, I decided to pursue fine arts. I harbored a lot of guilt for wanting to follow a path with uncertain pay and limited opportunities; however, when I told my dad he encouraged me to try anyways. My dad’s guidance and reassurance gave me the courage to strive for my goals.
When it came time to put together my portfolio, I realized I was short one piece. While reflecting on my dad’s role in my life and the hard work he has put into supporting our family, I was inspired me to make this painting. I named it after a song we listened to together, which he didn’t like much but listened to anyways because I wanted him to hear it. The song is Heart Emoji // Good Parenting by the band Guitar Fight from Fooly Cooly.

title: Projects
text:
Completed Project:

Impact of party affiliation on Americans’ level of trust in media.
COURSE PROJECT (PARTNERED PROJECT) · 2026
Role: Co-Author
Question: To what extent does one’s party affiliation influence their level of trust in mainstream media?
Variables:
IV: Party ID (Party Affiliation)
DV: Level of trust in Media
Hypotheses:
H₁ - Those who identify as Republicans are more likely than those who identify as Democrats to distrust the media.
H₂ - When controlling for trust in the federal government, we expect that party identification will have an interactive relationship with trust in the media. We expect that democrats with low trust in government will have a less significant decrease in trust in media than their Republican counterparts.
Approach: Used R to analyze National Elections Data set and test significance of relationship between IV and DV.
Findings:
overview: The percentage of Republicans who responded that they have no trust in the media was significantly higher than the percentage of their Democrat counterparts. 57.24% of Republicans report no trust in the media, compared with 10.71% of Democrats.
Significance: When we performed a test of significance, we found that Republicans are between 44.2 and 48.8 percentage points more likely to have no trust in the media compared to Democrats. Our p-value was well below 0.05 at 2.53 × 10⁻²⁴⁰; therefore, we rejected the null hypothesis and supported our claim that Americans’ party affiliations impact their levels of trust in the media.
Control: Contrary to our hypothesis, we found that, when controlling for trust in the federal government, republicans’ level of distrust in media remains consistent across frequency of trust in government.
